To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
transplantation of more mature hematopoietic progenitor cells can more rapidly correct immunodeficiency disorders in unconditioned mice.

transplantation of more mature flk2+ lymphoid-restricted progenitors can correct lymphoid deficiencies without the need for myelosuppressive conditioning, but that the use of more mature progenitors may limit the long-term immune reconstitutive capacity of the recipient.
transplantation of non-self-renewal multipotent progenitors can be used to correct lymphoid deficiencies without the use of myeloablative conditioning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing new therapies for the correction of hematopoietic deficiencies and disorders.
the development of novel strategies for the replacement of abnormal stem cells in a variety of diseases.
the development of new strategies to correct the genetic defects that underlie many forms of hematopoietic malignancy and immunodeficiency.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
flk2(+) cells are multipotent, non-self renewing progenitors that can be used to correct lymphoid deficiencies.
the use of non-self-renewable progenitors for the correction of lymphoid defects in unconditioned hosts is a feasible alternative to HSC transplantation.
transplantation of more mature progenitor cells is an alternative to the use of HSCs for the treatment of lymphoid disorders in unconditioned recipients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
transplantation of more mature progenitor cells can provide rapid lymphocyte reconstitution of unconditioned immunodeficient mice.

the use of more differentiated progenitors can provide a rapid means of lymphoid engraftment in immunodeficient hosts, and, in contrast to the use of HSCs, can be achieved without the need for cytoreductive conditioning.

the transplantation of flk2+/lin- progenitor cells is capable of correcting lymphoid deficiencies, and that the use of non-self-renewal multipotent progenitors may be a useful alternative to the replacement of HSCs in the future.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the transplantation of more differentiated hematopoietic progenitor cells can rapidly restore lymphoid deficiencies in immunodeficient mice.
more differentiated progenitor populations can be used to rescue lymphoid deficiencies in immunodeficient mice.
transplantation of non-self-renewal multipotent progenitors can rapidly correct lymphoid deficiency in unconditioned mice.
